chapter: Arranging for other bandleaders and closing talk
title: Claude Hopkins and the first reading of 'Christopher Columbus'
summary: Hopkins, who played the Roseland's second bandstand and had singer Orlando Robinson, played Horace's score first when Horace took it uptown before showing Fletcher.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Huh. That's really great. We've got a little tape here left. How about Claude Hopkins?

Claude Hopkins. I knew Claude Hopkins from the Roseland in New York. In fact, Claude used to play on Fletcher's bandstand, you know, because they always had two bandstands there in the Roseland right beside each other, you know. Facing This is the ballroom. And like Fletcher would go out on tours or go somewhere else. Then they'd we'd bring Claude Hopkins in, one of those things. This is how I met Claude, our first (unintelligible), and he had a good band. He had a great singer with him called Orlando Robeson. Don't know if you remember -- he sang sweet, and he reminded you a little bit of Billy Eckstine at the time. And Claude had good personnel in his band. He had some

good trumpet players, you know, ad lib men at the (unintelligible). And he later moved up into the Cotton Club up at Harlem at 143rd and Lenox Avenue or somewhere near the Savoy, something (unintelligible), you know, and he was playing for that great review at that time. And I remember Claude real well for one thing. The time that this Christopher Columbus came out. This is the riff that Chu Berry used to play and we talked about me making 32 bars out of. Well, I asked him, "Chu, do you mind me making 32 bars out of this riff you play so often?" He'd damn play...
-- seemed like it was a pattern with Chu, you know. He lifted the band with that. So I put a bridge in the thing and made 32 out of it.
Then I had the trumpets, you know --
-- one of those things. Claude Hopkins was the first band that ever played that.

For this reason -- when I finished copied the arrangement, and I got in my own score at that time. I wasn't able to have a copyist it copied, you know. I took it up to Claude before I took it down to Fletcher. And his band could read and everything, and, man, they went wild over the thing. and so he said, "Hey, I want this." Well, I says, "Well, okay. pass it in. I'll bring it back, you know, something. I was
on my way down to the Roseland, you know, to take it to Fletcher (Unintelligible) anyway. This is what happened.
I see. I'm going to change tapes here.
